دير آبانDayr Aban

The village as it was in 1948, rebuilt on the British survey sheet (surveyed 1931 and 1933, printed 1945): the ground from a modern elevation model checked against the survey points, the houses in the built-up areas the survey drew plus an estimated growth up to 1948, and the places named from the village book and its people's testimonies.

Jerusalem sub-district, at about 300 m. 1,534 people in 321 houses in 1931; 2,100 people in the 1945 statistics. The model shows …, a count that results from laying houses along the lanes, not a target. Depopulated on 19–20 October 1948.

About the work and the sources

A 3D model of the village of Dayr Aban (Jerusalem district) as it was before its people were driven out on 19–20 October 1948: the houses, lanes and squares, the land and its olive groves, and the place names, with guided walks. What has a documented position is shown there; what does not is shown as a approximate area or left without a position, never guessed. The number and layout of the houses are an estimate close to the statistics, not a drawing of each actual house.

By Hatem Abdallah Hasan Abd al-Nabi Salama.

Sources

  • Abd al-Aziz Abu Hudba, «A study of Palestinian society and folk heritage: the village of Dayr Aban» (in Arabic); "p." refers to its pages, including its hand-drawn maps (pp.180, 188, 192, 195, 300).
  • British 1:20,000 maps of Palestine (surveyed 1931–1933, printed 1945), sheets 14/12, 15/12 and 14/13, through Palestine Open Maps and scanned copies.
  • Salman H. Abu-Sitta, Atlas of Palestine 1917–1966, Palestine Land Society, London, 2010, pp.422–423.
  • Villagers' testimonies in the book; Abu Majdi (Yusuf Abd al-Hafiz Ali Husayn, born 1938); the Zochrot tour report and booklet «Remembering Dayr Aban» (2015).
  • The 1948 photos and the 1938 photo: Zochrot archive.
  • Ground: a modern elevation model checked against the survey points, and Copernicus 30 m for the far ground; the neighbouring villages from Palestine Open Maps, checked against Wikipedia.

The change log at the bottom of this panel gives the source and date of every change.

Photo of the 2nd Battalion, King's Own Royal Regiment, no. KO1021/03-084, held by the regiment's museum in Lancaster; it is not shown here without the museum's permission. The view matches the camera position and direction (333°, 47° wide) found from the skyline. Museum website

The June 1946 walk

The walk as the village book tells it (pp.178–181): the road to the village, the western entrance, the heart of the village, then al-Qati' and al-Batin. Landmarks are documented from the map; house positions are approximate, from the book's order and directions.

The lands tour: the places the book's ten farm roads pass (pp.193–197), from the village outwards; each stop names the road or roads that pass it; no neighbouring villages. Stops stand at register positions; names with no position are listed in the stop text and are not guessed. Places beyond the model terrain are viewed from its edge. A view from above, with a small map of the road.

Display

15:00

Ground colours: light earth is fallow and pasture (the map does not detail its plants), trees are olives where the 1945 map draws them, and the terraces round the village are cultivated. Blue lines are named wadis; the purple line is the village boundary where the map draws it clearly.

Tap any building to see its ID, footprint and the names mentioned along that part of the walk: a possible area, never the owner of a specific roof.

Documented positionApproximate position

The master register (3 October 2026)

Every place with a position in the master register has a pin coloured by its confidence. Tap a pin to see its source and pages. Settled rules: the course of Wadi Qurayqi' as in the register; no house in the Qurayqi' or Shi'b beds; only al-Batin north of Qurayqi'; al-Qati' as a approximate area south of the separating road.

Adjustable assumption: the house-free width of the two beds (, for Qurayqi' and the Shi'b) is our estimate, not a measurement from the sources; the register gives position accuracy (±40 and ±50 m), not channel width. Houses kept out of the beds were re-sited along the lanes on their banks (within 40 m).

From the villagers' testimonies
شارع الصوانه، كان كله صبر على الجهتينAbu Majdi, Yusuf 'Abd al-Hafiz 'Ali Husayn (born 1938): "al-Sawwana street was all prickly pear on both sides"
من وسط البلد لفوق، كان اسمه الجامع العمريAbu Majdi: "from the middle of the village upwards, it was called al-'Umari mosque"
كان بالبلد مدرسة وجامع وعين عليها 12 حنفيةHajja Fatima 'Abdallah Ibrahim (born c.1929): "the village had a school, a mosque, and a spring with 12 taps"
يا قمح يا ديرباني يا طالع ع الميّهFrom the harvest songs, as Hajja Fatima sang them

Source: «Remembering Dayr Aban», Zochrot, 2015. Quotes kept in the original Arabic.

Index of the master register ()

Every name in the master register (houses, places, land, landmarks, families and persons), with the book pages where it occurs and its confidence. Tap a name that has a position to fly to it. Names are in Arabic, as in the book.

Dar Ziyada (Dar Abd Ziyada) is of Ibn Hudhayl; its house is at the west end of al-Qati', where the separating road begins, and the village's only sycamore stood there (pp.181, 206, 259, 365). Dar Ziyad is of al-Da'amsa, and "Zahr Dar Ziyad", the hill west of the village south of the station, is named after it. The register called the hill "Zahr Abu Ziyad"; the name is corrected, and the hill now links to 12 pages of the book. Its position fits the station, Khirbat Alin and Ein al-Bassa (pp.214, 361, 363). Dar Abd al-Aziz Suwayd and Harat Dar Suwayd are in the east of al-Qati', south of the Ibn Hudhayl quarter, to which the Suwayd family belongs (pp.61, 181, 221). No position changed.
    • 3 October 2026 (al-Ghurus and Abajul): neither has a position in the register, and none was guessed. What the book gives is relative. Al-Ghurus is "in the south of the village" (p.206), on Wadi Abu Khashaba where Wadi Qit'at al-Umari joins it (p.189), and Wadi al-Ghurus comes from Wadi al-Tin, the boundary between the lands of Jarash and Dayr Aban (pp.193, 197). Abajul is at the southern end of the ridge west of the village (p.185); al-Kabir belongs to Jarash and al-Saghir to Dayr Aban, and it lies west of al-Ghurus on the boundary (p.193). Both are south and south-west of al-Qati' (p.197), between Jurun al-Hanun and Niyata. The "al-'Arus" pin is now marked inferred, not documented: the name is the previous model's reading of "El 'Asharāt?" on the 1945 map, and the book does not mention it.
    • 3 October 2026 (the boundary between al-Qati' and al-Balad): Jurun al-Qaramla lay "between al-Balad and al-Qati'", at al-Mahwara and at Dar Farhan Ja'ara (pp.201, 253), but it stood about 21 m inside al-Qati'. It has moved to the edge of the separating road. The west edge of the probable al-Qati' area was corrected: Dar Uthman Ja'ara, one of the western houses of al-Qati' (p.181), is now inside it. Dar Mustafa Shurayyim and al-Qusayr are now outside, because Dar Mustafa Shurayyim and Jurun al-Hanun are "west of al-Qati'" (pp.196–197, 201, 253). The south edge is still drawn, not sourced: the book names al-Ghurus and Abajul south of al-Qati' (p.197), and neither has a position in the register.
    • 3 October 2026 (houses near the Shi'b line): the schematic line of Shi'b al-Husaynat cut diagonally from Hajar al-Sawwan to al-Mahwara through the middle of the Qaramla and Diyariba houses, so ten register houses were less than 15 m from it. But p.189 has the Shi'b pass "Hajar al-Sawwan between al-Qati' and al-Balad", then al-Mahwara, then Jurun al-Qaramla, then north along the eastern edge of al-Marj. It now runs along the separating road, which is the boundary between al-Qati' and al-Balad, then to the threshing floors, then north to al-Marj between the Ziyada houses. No register house is now less than 10 m from it. The west end of the separating road was also corrected: it passed north of Dar Isa Muhaysin and Bad al-Munirin, counting them in al-Qati', though both are in Harat al-Diyariba in al-Balad (pp.179, 205). It now passes south of them, and it drops slightly at al-Shaykh Abdallah so that this stays in the village centre (pp.232, 294). Jurun al-Qaramla moved slightly south to stay south of the road (pp.181, 365). Both lines remain inferred.
    • 3 October 2026 (Hajar al-Sawwan): p.181 gives the order coming down from al-Qati': the poet's house, then Hajar al-Sawwan, then the Ibn Hudhayl quarter. P.189 puts it on the Shi'b "between al-Qati' and al-Balad". Pp.259 and 391 speak of "the Hajar al-Sawwan road", which runs east of al-Mahwara to al-Qaramla and Ibn Hudhayl; there the name is the road's, not the stone's position. The stone stood east of the Ibn Hudhayl saha, so the p.181 walk doubled back west after it. It has moved to the boundary between al-Qati' and al-Balad, between the poet's house and the Ibn Hudhayl quarter. The position remains inferred until a villager confirms it.
    • 3 October 2026: the village's only oven (Faris Abd al-Qadir's, p.179) and the shops and barbershops were drawn far smaller than an ordinary room: a shop was 4 × 3.6 m and 3 m high, and the oven a 3 × 3 m hut. A shop, barbershop or butcher's shop is now a vaulted room 6 × 5 m and 4 m high, and the oven a room 6.5 × 5.5 m with a 3.6 m wall and a dome. These are estimated sizes for a vaulted village room, not measurements from the book.
    • 3 October 2026 (the houses of al-Balad from the book): the Da'amsa saha, in the house of the Mukhtar Hasan Abu Hudba, stood at the west end, 200 m from the mosque, following a figure on p.47. But p.178 puts it after al-Mahwara, on the left as one goes into the centre. On p.259 a Da'amsa groom's procession goes from Dar Farhan Ja'ara "along the al-Mahwara road to the village centre until it reaches the Da'amsa saha in Dar Hasan Abu Hudba". P.205 puts the Abu Hudba olive press near Dar Khalil Ja'ara, and Abu Majdi's testimony puts Dar Abu Hudba and its press below the Umari. So the Mukhtar's house is now Dar Abu Hudba (p.47: the radio sat on its veranda "facing the hosh and the well grove"; p.253: "the well grove of Dar Abu Hudba"), and the saha has moved to it. The 200 m figure stays open until a villager confirms it. The Ibn Hudhayl saha, which was south of the separating road in al-Qati', has moved south of al-Mashar near Dar Abd al-Mun'im (pp.47, 222, 259). The wedding square has moved slightly north, so that it is north-east of the Umari (p.253). The other houses of al-Balad match the book: the Dar Awda press east of Dar Abd Ahmad near al-Mashar, Bad al-Munirin near Dar Isa Muhaysin (p.205), and al-Shaykh Abdallah between the Ibn Hudhayl and Qaramla quarters (p.294). There are 359 dwellings, slightly above the agreed 330–350: the generator uses one random sequence for the whole village, so moving these named buildings redistributed the houses (v7 had 348). The count was not forced.
    • 3 October 2026 (the houses of al-Qati' from the book): the p.181 walk through al-Qati' matches the register: from the crossroads, Dar Ziyada, Dar Uthman Ja'ara and Dar Abu Salama to the west, then a little higher Dar Da'san and Dar al-Baz, then east Dar Abd al-Aziz Suwayd and Dar Mahmud Khalif. Three corrections: (1) Jurun al-Qaramla (al-Mashaniq) sat on the separating road itself, while the book has us cross the road southwards from Bab al-Mahwara and then see the floors (p.181), which lie "between Dar Abd Ziyada and al-Mahwara" (p.365); the west end of the inferred separating road now climbs from Dar Ziyada and runs between al-Mahwara (north) and the floors (south). (2) Dar Mustafa Muhammad Uthman (the poet) is "in al-Balad" after the road drops out of al-Qati' (p.181), and he was of al-Qaramla (p.49); it stood south of the road, in al-Qati', and now stands north of it at the edge of the Qaramla houses. (3) Dar Awadallah Ashrim is added at the west edge before Dar Ziyada (p.259: the procession goes south from al-Marj near Dar Awadallah Ashrim, then Dar Ziyada, then Jurun al-Qaramla). (4) Houses west of Dar Ziyada, where the separating road begins, were counted in al-Balad; they are the west part of al-Qati' (pp.181, 206), so Dar Ziyada, Dar Uthman Ja'ara and Dar Awadallah Ashrim now count in al-Qati'. Still open: Hajar al-Sawwan, which pp.259 and 391 put on the road east of al-Mahwara before the Qaramla quarter, while the register keeps it east of al-Qaramla near Ibn Hudhayl, following the p.181 order.
    • 3 October 2026 (the houses of al-Batin from the book): p.181: past Jurun al-Masan "al-Batin is on our right" and the school on the left as we walk north on the Jinna'ir road, so al-Batin lies east of the road. P.253: wedding evenings "at Jurun al-Masan near Dar Khraywish and Dar Hasan Salih Sa'ada". Dar Hasan Salih Sa'ada moves from west of the road (inside the threshing-floor circle) to its east side, facing the floors, with Dar Khraywish beside it. Every house the book names in al-Batin now has its own building and pin (Khraywish, Abdallah Ubayd, Ali Hasan, As'ad Sa'ada, Amira, Hasan Salih Sa'ada, Abdallah Hamdan) instead of one "houses of al-Batin" group; the last five are approximate within al-Batin, since the book does not place them. Dar Abdallah Hamdan, "at the top of the hill", now stands on the crest of the raised spur east of al-Batin (about 300 m) instead of its lower earlier spot: a reading of the text, not a measurement. Note: on p.222 the barber "Ali Hasan Awadallah in old al-Masa'id" may be a different person from the house in al-Batin.
    • 3 October 2026 (the 1946 walk from the book): the walk was rebuilt from the text of pp.178–181 in its order, so every house, saha or quarter the book names is its own stop instead of grouped stops: 99 stops instead of 73. Added: the al-'Umari and Dar al-Sandaqa squares, the wedding square and Dar Muhammad Hasan Ibrahim, al-Sadduq and Dar Abd al-Aziz Yusuf, al-Da'amsa and Dar Abdallah Hussein, al-Kasabira and the gateways of Dar Awda, the view from al-Mashar, Dar Ali Hussein and Dar Abd Ahmad, the Ibn Hudhayl quarter and its saha, Dar Isa Muhaysin, the al-Qaramla saha, the houses of al-Qati' (Ziyada, Uthman Ja'ara, Abu Salama, Da'san, al-Baz, Abd al-Aziz Suwayd, Mahmud Khalif), Dar Bayyud and Dar Abd al-Hafiz Khalil, Dar Sa'ada and Dar Abu al-Kara'in, the seven houses of al-Batin, and the al-Wa'ra cemetery and the saint Abu Hasan as two stops. Dar Khraywish, Abdallah Ubayd, Ali Hasan, As'ad Sa'ada and the road to the al-Wa'ra cemetery are approximate (no register position). The al-Wa'ra section: the al-Wa'ra walk now has 21 stops, adding the houses of the al-Wa'ra families (p.152 and the index: Ashrim, Abd al-Dayim, al-Bayza with Rashid, Bayyud and Amira), Dar Sa'ada and Dar Abu al-Kara'in facing Dar al-'Abd Salama, and the road to the al-Wa'ra cemetery and the saint Abu Hasan; the Jurun al-Masan label is moved to its place north of the wadi; and the al-Wa'ra groom's procession starts on the al-Mahwara road (p.259), not "al-Hadura".
    • 3 October 2026 (book review): p.47: a clan 'saha' is a guest room (madafa), not an open square, so the sahas of al-Da'amsa (in the house of the Mukhtar Hasan Abu Hudba), al-Qaramla, Ibn Hudhayl and old al-Wa'ra are now rooms. Pp.179, 222–224: the village market ran from al-'Umari to al-Shaykh Abdallah; Nimr Shurayyim's shop and Uthman Mas'ad's barbershop north of the al-'Umari square, Mahmud al-Baz's shop and Mustafa al-Rabiba's barbershop east of it facing the mosque's eastern domes, with the Sharabati shops, Ali al-Ghazal's barbershop and Abu Hashim al-Yazuri's butcher's shop; Fayyad al-Khalili's shop under the 'alali of Muhammad Hussein Adwan, and Atiyya the shoemaker opposite al-Shaykh Abdallah. P.178: houses on al-Natisha and in the Da'amsa threshing floors. Pp.181, 241: Dar Amira and Dar Hasan Salih Sa'ada in al-Batin, and Dar al-Baz in al-Qati' as modern buildings. Pp.239–240: a saqifa and a tabun in the hosh, verandas on columns in front of the 'alali, and more cross-vaulted houses in al-Qati' and al-Batin.
    • 3 October 2026: every register name that stands for a building now has one at its position: 71 named buildings (the houses, including Dar al-'Abd Salama as a large house and the gateways of Dar Awda as houses round a court with a gate, the shops and the two barbershops at the al-'Umari square, the one oven, and the olive presses). The 'alali are two storeys, as on p.241. The fig gardens (hawakir al-tin) are fig trees without houses, the remains of the Roman monastery are a few low walls at the edge of the wedding square (p.179), and the squares stay open. The hosh is the building unit of al-Balad, while most houses in al-Batin, al-Qati' and the lower village have almost none (pp.239–240), so most al-Balad houses have at least a small hosh and few in al-Batin and al-Qati' do. The generator makes a second pass over all the village lanes to fill gaps.
    • 3 October 2026: places and index from the master register (data/master_register.json), the single reference. Colours: green documented (explicit text or map), blue oral testimony, orange inferred. Names without a position appear in the index only.

    From the sources

    • Wadi Qurayqi': the course is documented, the position ±40 m (the faint band). The water tank is south of it and the school north of it (p.233). Its bed (±10 m) and the Shi'b al-Husaynat bed (±6 m, schematic line) are kept free of generated houses; both widths are an adjustable assumption, not a measurement. The generator then ran a second pass along the lanes on the banks of the two channels only (within 40 m) to re-site the displaced houses.
    • Separate counts: dwellings (the main house of a compound, a single house or a house in a joined row), house groups, annexes (attached rooms and small outbuildings), and public or landmark buildings. The count results from laying houses along the lanes, not a target; the agreed range is 330–350 dwellings.
    • Only al-Batin lies north of Qurayqi' (Mahseya is built over it): every generated house north of the line counts as al-Batin, and no al-Batin house lies south of it. South of the separating road (from Dar Ziyada to the cemetery) counts as al-Qati'.
    • Al-Qati' is a approximate area without documented limits: its west end is S-SW of al-'Umari, behind the Derech Eretz venue (31.74175 N, 35.00923 E). No source places it on hill 404D.
    • The 1946 walk and the al-Wa'ra section: every stop or place with a name in the register now stands at its register position (24 stops moved, including the school, Jurun al-Masan and the al-Batin houses), and Jurun al-Masan is now north of the wadi as on p.233. No generated house stands on a road, a lane or the separating road, and roads stop at the walls of public buildings.
    • Still open: 10 houses near the schematic Shi'b line, until villagers confirm the channel's course.
    • Ground: the Copernicus 30 m elevation model (a modern radar survey) on the Palestine Grid (EPSG:28191), checked against the survey points of the sheets; around the village they agree to about a metre. Summits were restored to their recorded heights, and the map's contours (from the 1918 survey at 1:40,000) were used on Jebel Haraza, quarried after 1945. The ground now extends about 1.2 km west and 1.5 km north, and is fitted to the points of sheet 14/12: the station platform 391c (213.6 m; the modern model was 1.3 m low), 405D (245.0 m; 3.9 m low) and 389c (313.7 m; 0.7 m low). The quarry runs north of the old edge (at 429D the sheet gives 409.0 m, the ground today 371.5 m), so the pit there is filled with a smooth surface between the restored edge and undisturbed ground, never below today's surface; an estimate, not traced contours. Modern building bumps (Beit Shemesh and the industrial zone, about 0.35 km², up to 9.9 m) were removed from the added ground west of the quarry only. Tiles N31 E034 and N31 E035 cover the whole area.
    • House limits: the six red built-up areas on that sheet (surveyed 1931–1933), split between al-Balad and al-Qati' as in the village book's plans.
    • The mosque, main cemetery, school, water tank, threshing floors, Maqam Abu Hasan, the mill, the springs, the olive groves and the wadis: from the map, confirmed by the book's plans and the Zochrot booklet.
    • Quarters: al-Qati' in the south, al-Batin in the north, al-Balad between them.

    Reconstructed

    • Individual houses are generated inside the built-up areas; their real layout is not yet known, and families can help through the house sheet and the square grid.
    • Al-Batin's houses are not drawn on the map; they are placed along the road towards the school as on the book's plan, and on the hill north of Wadi Qureiqi', east of the Jinna'ir road.
    • House layout (revised after the p.180 sketch, the pp.178–181 walk and the photos): the lanes come first (the six roads of the survey sheet, lanes following the contours inside the built-up areas, and climbing paths between them no steeper than 35%), then family compounds beside them: a one- or two-level house, an attached room, a walled courtyard and sometimes a small outbuilding. Al-Balad and al-Qati' are dense inside the 1931–33 survey areas, with narrow passages and empty plots; beyond them houses are scattered, and only in growth zones where the photos show houses: south of al-Qati' (1938 photo), the west, south-west and north slope (1948 photos), and the al-Batin strip on the Jinnair road (sketch). Not every sketch mark is a house and there is no target number: the model has . This is separate from the text's house count (321 houses in 1931, p.21) and from the sketch's marks (about 184 schematic symbols). Ground steeper than 42% and drainage lines are left open, and no house straddles more than 3 m of slope.
    • The book's sketch (p.180) on the ground: drawn from memory without scale; a single rotation and scale misses by 142 m on average (251 m at the mill), because the core is drawn enlarged and the edges squeezed. So it is pinned at seven points and warped between them: the mosque, school, main cemetery, Maqam Abu Hasan and the mill from the 1945 sheet; al-Mashar and al-Shaykh 'Abdallah approximate. It is shown only as a comparison layer (roads, cluster edges, empty ground), not as house positions. The top of the sketch points south-east (about 125°); the 'Overhead, turned like the p.180 sketch' button turns the view the same way.
    • Landmarks: al-'Umari mosque at the 'M.' of the 1945 sheet (about 6 m) with its square on the north (pp.290–292); the main cemetery at 'Cem.'; the school moved to the building symbol inside the school enclosure on the sheet (±10 m; it was at the enclosure corner, 70 m away); the water tank at 'W.T.', which p.21 contradicts (hypothesis); al-Mashar at survey point 403D (hypothesis: the high flat place; the sketch puts it at the east edge near the cemetery); Dar al-'Abd Salama: a search area on the route from the old al-Wa'ra square toward the new al-Masa'id quarter, opposite Dar Sa'ada and Dar Abu al-Kara'in (p.181), with no roof chosen.
    • Building IDs: every building has an ID fixed for this version, from the squares of the family house sheet (e.g. K12-3; a, b, c for the buildings of one compound). Tapping a building lists the names mentioned near it on the walk, with their pages, as a possible area; no name is assigned to a specific roof.
    • The ground is not reshaped to fit the houses: the terrace stepping was removed from the ground surface (it shifted it by up to about 2.8 m), so the hillside is the elevation model itself; field terrace walls are drawn as low walls on that surface, on moderate slopes outside the house areas only.
    • Look of the houses and trees, from the photographs of the surviving houses: rough, undressed limestone; roughly squared blocks of uneven size in irregular courses, with small stones in the joints and earthen mortar; packed-earth roofs; pointed-arch doorways; whitewashed domes on some houses. Around the houses dense prickly pear, and almond, carob, fig and olive on the terraces; pines, cypress and eucalyptus planted on the village edges before 1948 (p.206, Abu Majdi). The 'today' layer: roofless standing walls and rubble heaps.
    • Settled by book pages 183–226 and the Zochrot booklet: Dabbat al-Tantura lies west of 'the Tantura bridge', south of the railway (p.194), and 'Abu Tantur' north of the line is another place; Wadi al-Khaniq runs north of the village between Abu Hasan and Jinna'ir (p.189, Zochrot); Dhahr Abu Ziyad is 'Dhahr Dar Ziyad', west of the village and south of al-Rayyan (pp.189, 205, 217), from where the Jewish forces fired; the bakery was most likely 'Abd al-Qadir al-Shaykh's, with Faris his son; the water tank stood on the edge of Wadi Qureiqi' by the school, taps on the south and troughs on the west (p.215). Still open: 'Ayn Marjalayn at 1.6 km on the map against '5 km' in Zochrot (the book gives the distance by the rough road); Dar Hasan 'Ubayd at the al-Wa'ra square (p.179) or 'on another hill' (Abu Majdi); threshing floors and mill 'in the east' in Zochrot but in the west in the book and on the map.
    • Al-'Umari mosque (pp.290–291), rebuilt from the book's description and drawing: the tomb room of Sheikh Ahmad al-'Umari (4 x 3 m) jutting south under a small dome; the arcades (4 x 4 m bays) with three domes and three arches onto the square; the three-storey raised building (the guest room 8 x 8 m and 4 m high, the third storey with loopholes) and its unfinished vault; and the square on the north with its entrance, the well in its south-west, the two al-Nuwayhi graves and the ablution place. Dimensions the book does not give are estimates, and the building is assumed to sit square to north and south.
    • Clan zones (pp.44–45), from the book's sketch of how the village grew: A al-Diyariyya, B al-Qaramila, C Ibn Hudhayl, D al-Da'amsa with al-Suduq and al-Masa'id, E al-Kasabira, F al-Wa'ra, plus the spreads into al-Qati', al-Batin and the west. They are rough zones around the mosque, not house boundaries.
    • Name lines: during the walk each stop shows only the named houses near it (up to 7), outlined and numbered, with a line to each name and a small top-down map; outside the walk you can tap any house, or switch on the names of nearby houses (up to 8).
    • From p.21: 1,214 people in 1922 and 1,534 in 1931 (752 men, 782 women) in 321 houses; the village covered 54 dunums, built 'radially' with five streets meeting in the centre (the model has six roads, from the 1945 map). New conflicts: the water 'collected in a tank in the middle of the village' (p.21) against the tank at the bottom of the village on the west, by the school (pp.214–215); the al-Suduq and al-Da'amsa quarters on the right going up to al-Mashar (p.179), while the p.45 sketch puts their zone to the north-east; village lands of 22,748 dunums (p.21) against 22,734 (Zochrot).
    • The 1938 view: camera position (31.7404890, 35.0102529) and direction from matching the skyline to the terrain; approximate.
    • Names index: 'documented' from the 1945 map or the book's plans, 'approximate' from the walk's order and directions, 'outside the model' at the edge, 'not yet placed' where no position is set yet; uncertain handwritten readings are marked. 'Family' entries come from the families table (pp.60–61).
    • Roads are drawn by eye; al-Mashar, al-Shaykh 'Abdallah, the olive presses, the standing house and the 'today' layer are approximate.
    • The 1946 walk: the order and directions of the stops come from the book; house positions on it are approximate. Dabbat al-Tantura's position comes from the book's text (p.194); the al-Safiya crossroads is inferred from the book and the Bureij sheet. The station, police post, level crossing and al-Safiya are now on the ground at their positions on sheets 14/12 and 14/13; only Bab al-Wad and the lands of Bayt Mahsir, 'Islin, Ishwa' and Sar'a lie beyond it, pointed to from the road.
    • The north-west (sheets 14/12, 14/13 1942 edition and 15/13 1943 edition, registered on their 1 km grids to 2–3 m): the whole railway is traced from the sheets and rides over the wadis on a smoothed grade instead of dipping into them. The station: the sheet shows two tracks and a siding from the level crossing to about 650 m east of it; they are laid about 5 m apart, true to life, because the map symbol spreads them about 20 m. The station building, goods shed, two staff houses and platform are at their symbols; their form (stone, tiled roofs) is generic, not from a photograph. The police post: building and compound wall at their mapped positions; the building's form is generic. The iron bridge over Wadi al-Sarar: position from the sheet ('Iron'); the truss is generic. The Tantura bridge: the sheet shows a stone railway bridge over Wadi Abu Khashaba ('Stone'); calling it Jisr al-Tantura is an inference from p.194 (the dabba west of it and south of the line); the arches are generic. Har Tuv and Artuf: houses in the built-up areas and along the street as mapped; their number and forms are estimates. The village's own house outlines come from an earlier registration about 7 m off this grid, within the stated margin, and are left unchanged.
    • Photo angles and lenses are estimates; use the blend and lens controls to judge for yourself.
    Sources
    • British survey of Palestine 1:20,000, sheet 15/12 'Deir Esh Sheikh': topographic survey 1931 and 1933, plantations revised 1932–1934, roads to December 1942, contours from the 1918 survey, printed 1945. Sheets 14/12 'Bureij', 14/13 'Latrun' (1942 edition, not the 1948 reprint with Hebrew overprint) and 15/13 'Bab el Wad' (1943) for the station, police post, road, Har Tuv and Artuf, from the Palestine Open Maps pom-data index.
    • Copernicus GLO-30 elevation model, tiles N31 E034 and N31 E035 (European Space Agency).
    • 'Abd al-'Aziz Abu Hudba, «Qaryat Dayraban» (pp.21, 44–45, 60–61, 174–226, 232, 243, 290–293).
    • Zochrot, «Remembering Dayr Aban» (2015), with the testimonies of Abu Majdi and Hajja Fatima.
    • Survey of Western Palestine (1883); Village Statistics 1945; Walid Khalidi, «All That Remains» (1992).
    • The railway: traced from the same four sheets (previously the digitised Palestine Open Maps line, which ran 10–15 m south of the printed track near the station).
    • The four 1948 photos and the Google Earth views you sent.

    Dayr Aban

    An attempt to rebuild the village in three dimensions

    Initial release

    This work seeks to rebuild the village of Dayr Aban in three dimensions, based on what Mr Abd al-Aziz Abu Hudba documented in his book "The Village of Dayr Aban", and with the help of historical maps, photographs, testimonies and other sources, to bring back the village's landmarks, houses, quarters, roads and lands.

    However much effort has gone into gathering, checking and linking the information, the work still contains estimates and possible errors. We welcome remarks from the people of the village, and any information and documents they hold, to help correct it, develop it and bring it closer to the village as it really was. This is an initial release, to be updated whenever further information or evidence becomes available.

    Help us complete the historical picture of the village, its people and its houses, and correct any errors. To get in touch and send remarks, see «Contact & feedback» at the end of the menu.
